title: How to play
text: Path Tracer is a library of short explainer videos on the methods behind biosocial science: how evolution shapes behaviour, how twins reveal heritability, how genome-wide studies find genes, how penalized regression tames a million predictors, and how marks on DNA keep biological time.

title: How to play
text:
The rules of the game

Sectors are the big topics. Each one is a landscape of its own.
Levels are the episodes, 2–7 minutes each. Every level answers one question and ends on the next one.
Play a sector in order. Levels build on each other, and each one says up front which earlier levels it assumes.
Legendary levels are the advanced material at the end of each sector. They open once the core path is clear.
A level’s light tells you where it stands. Online levels are released. In production levels are being built. Locked levels are planned, and the map shows them anyway, so you can see where the game is going.

title: How to play
text:
The style
Two YouTube channels inspired the house style. StatQuest never skips a step, uses tiny examples and marks every payoff. 3Blue1Brown treats the picture as the argument and keeps the maths exactly right. Path Tracer tries for both: every symbol gets a picture before it gets notation, and nothing is simplified into something false.
The look is the Grid, a soft-glow homage to a certain light-cycle film. The name comes from Sewall Wright’s path tracing, the rules that turn a diagram of genes and environments into the equations of the twin model. The light cycle in the videos traces those same paths.

title: How to play
text:
Who makes it
Peter Tanksley, a research scientist who teaches biosocial criminology. Path Tracer is an evenings-and-weekends project. The videos are built in Manim Community Edition and this site in Quarto.

Where do the twin equations come from?
IN PRODUCTION 6-7 min

IN PRODUCTION






NoteThe maths, slowly





Draft — last updated October 23, 2026.
Put every variable on a standard scale, so each has variance 1. A twin’s score P is built from three latent sources, each with variance 1: additive genes A, shared environment C and unique environment E. The paths from them to P are a, c and e.
Wright’s tracing rules. The covariance between two variables is the sum, over every allowed chain between them, of the product of the path values along the chain. A chain may go backwards along arrows and then forwards, never forwards then backwards. It passes through at most one double-headed arrow, and it visits no variable twice.
One twin. A variable’s variance is its covariance with itself: the chains that leave P and come back.
\operatorname{Var}(P) = a^2 + c^2 + e^2 = 1
Identical (MZ) pairs. Twin 1’s A correlates 1 with twin 2’s A, and the C’s correlate 1. The E’s are not linked.
r_{MZ} = a^2 + c^2
Fraternal (DZ) pairs. The A’s correlate ½, because DZ twins share half their segregating genes on average. The C’s still correlate 1.
r_{DZ} = \tfrac{1}{2}a^2 + c^2
Subtract. The shared environment cancels:
r_{MZ} - r_{DZ} = \tfrac{1}{2}a^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad h^2 = a^2 = 2\,(r_{MZ} - r_{DZ})
With the running example (r_MZ = .70, r_DZ = .40): a² = .60, c² = .70 − .60 = .10, e² = 1 − .70 = .30.
